Atalanta. The huntress who would only marry a man who could outrun her. She was unique among Greek heroes for her determination to remain independent and unmarried, a skilled archer and runner of supernatural speed who was raised by Artemis and her nymphs after being exposed as an infant. Devoted to the goddess of the hunt, she swore an oath of chastity that would define her entire life. Her independence was extraordinary for a woman in an age when marriage and family were expected of everyone.

She earned her place in history in many ways. As the only woman to sail with Jason aboard the Argo in search of the Golden Fleece, she competed with the greatest male heroes and earned their respect as an equal. She sailed across unknown seas alongside legendary warriors. At the famous hunt for the Calydonian Boar, a monster of enormous power and ferocity, she was the only woman among the hunters, and she proved herself by striking the beast alongside warriors of legendary status. Her achievements earned her renown throughout the world of heroes.

But she is most remembered for her suitors and the impossible test she set for them. Atalanta vowed to marry only the man who could beat her in a footrace. To lose meant death. She defeated every single challenger, year after year, turning away man after man. Her fame grew. Then a clever suitor named Hippomenes appeared with an unexpected advantage. The goddess Aphrodite, the force of desire itself, had taken pity on him and given him three golden apples of extraordinary beauty. As Atalanta raced him, the shining fruit distracted her just enough for him to pull ahead and claim victory.

So she married Hippomenes. Yet their happiness was not to last. The couple showed disrespect toward the gods, and Aphrodite and Zeus took their vengeance. Both were transformed into lions, condemned to pull the chariot of the goddess Cybele for all eternity. Her story explores the themes of freedom, independence, and the cost of losing one's self to another, even through an act we call love.
